query: Hail in the Courtyard {Hail comes out of a clear sky, stones the size of peas, then the size of marbles. A knot of first-years is caught in the middle of the courtyard with their books over their heads.|Hail again, the courtyard's speciality. The first-years know to run now; they just don't know where.|The sky goes white and the hail comes down like a dropped tray of beads. {season == "summer": In summer, which is insulting.|The fountain rings with it.}} Herd them into the cloister {You wave them into the cloister and take the last of the hail on your own back. One of them gives you a sugar mouse from their pocket, warm and slightly squashed.|You get them all in and count them twice. Your ears ring for an hour from the stones.|You herd them like ducks into the cloister, the stones bouncing off your shoulders. One of them says thank you in a very small voice.} Run for cover yourself {You make the cloister in six strides and watch them work it out for themselves. They do, eventually, damply.|You run. A prefect gets them in. You feel you were quicker than you should have been.|Cover first. From the cloister you shout directions, which helps a little and makes you feel better a lot.} Raise a ward over them {You throw up a ward like a roof and the hail bounces off it in a white roar. The first-years stand under it, dry, looking up at you as if you'd hung the sky.|A pale shell over the knot of them. The hail drums on it like rain on a tent. Somebody under it starts to sing.|You walk them across the courtyard under a ward, slowly, like a procession. Half the castle is watching from the windows. You don't hurry.}
